Annual Meetings

Morning Session - 2016 Meeting

Warren Buffett is asked how Berkshire might be affected if Donald Trump is elected president. He and Charlie Munger also look at how Amazon has "disrupted plenty of people," and Buffett explains how GEICO is being affected by an increase in the automobile death rate, even as cars become safer.

Sat, Apr 30 2016 • 9:00 AM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 8. Precisions Castparts acquisition
  2. 11. Rise in auto death rate hurt GEICO
  3. 12. Amazon has "disrupted plenty of people"
  4. 13. Defending Coca-Cola from sugar health worries
  5. 15. Derivatives still a "danger to the system"
  6. 19. Nevada utility customers shouldn't have to subsidize solar power
  7. 22. Berkshire will "do fine" if Trump or Clinton wins
  8. 28. Sequoia Fund was "overly entranced" by Valeant

Sync Video to Paragraph

"In your 1987 letter to shareholders, you commented on the kind of companies Berkshire likes to buy, those that required only small amounts of capital. Sync Video to Paragraph

"Today the company has changed its strategy. It now invests in companies that need tons of capital expenditures, are overregulated, and earn lower returns on equity capital. Why did this happen?"

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah. Well, it's one of the problems of prosperity.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The ideal business is one that takes no capital, but yet grows, and there are a few businesses like that, and we own some.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But we are not able â we'd love to find one that we could buy for $10 or $20 or $30 billion that was not capital intensive and we may, but it's harder.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And that does â that does hurt us, in terms of compounding earnings growth, because, obviously, if you have a business that grows and gives you a lot of money every year and doesn't take it â it isn't required in its growth â you know, you get a double-barreled effect from the earnings growth that occurs internally without the use of capital, and then you get the capital it produces to go and buy other businesses. And See's Candy was a good example of that. I've used that.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Back when the newspaper business was good, our Buffalo newspaper was, for example, was a good example of that. The Buffalo newspaper was making, at one time, $40 million a year and had no capital requirement, so we could take that whole $40 million and go and do â go buy something else with it.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But capital â increasing capital â acts as an anchor on returns in many ways. And one of the ways is that it drives us into â just in terms of availability â it drives us into businesses that are much more capital intensive.

Sync Video to Paragraph

You just saw a slide, for example, on Berkshire Hathaway Energy, where we just announced, just in the last couple of weeks, we announced a $3.6 billion investment coming up in wind generation. And we pledged overall to have $30 billion in renewables.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Anything that Berkshire Hathaway Energy does, anything that BNSF does, takes lots of money. We get decent returns on capital, but we don't get the extraordinary returns on capital that we've been able to get in some of the businesses we acquire that are not capital intensive.

Sync Video to Paragraph

As I mentioned in the annual report, we have a few businesses that actually earn 100 percent a year on true invested capital. And clearly, that's a different sort of operation than something like Berkshire Hathaway Energy, which may earn 11 or 12 percent on capital â and that's a very decent return â but it's a different sort of animal than the business that's very low capital intensive â intensity.

Sync Video to Paragraph

10. Reinsurance outlook a factor in Munich Re and Swiss Re sales

WARREN BUFFETT: OK, Becky Quick.

Sync Video to Paragraph

BECKY QUICK: This question comes from Solomon Ackerman, who's in Frankfurt, Germany.

Sync Video to Paragraph

He wants to know why Berkshire has significantly sold down their holdings in Munich Re, which is the world's biggest reinsurance company, based in Germany, while sticking with the reinsurance operations within Berkshire, like Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance and General Re.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Would you reduce exposure to Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance and General Re if they were listed companies? And he's hoping that this can bring out some of your insights as to what's happening in the reinsurance business right now.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah, we â I said in the annual report that I thought it was very likely that the reinsurance business would not be as good in the next ten years as it has been in the last ten years.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I may be wrong on that, but that's just a judgment based on seeing the competitive dynamics of the reinsurance business now versus 10 or 20 years ago.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Both Munich â we sold our entire holdings, which were substantial â of Munich Re and Swiss Re. We owned about 3 percent of Swiss Re, and we own more than 10 percent of Munich Re, and last year we sold those two holdings.

Sync Video to Paragraph

They're fine companies. They're well-managed companies. I like the people that run them.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I think their business â the business of the reinsurance companies generally â is less attractive for the next 10 years than it has been for the last 10 years.

Sync Video to Paragraph

In part, that's because what's happened to interest rates. A significant portion of what you earn in insurance comes from investment of the float. And both of those companies, and for that matter almost all of the reinsurance industry, is somewhat more restricted in what they can do with their float, because they don't have this huge capital cushion that Berkshire has, and also because they don't have this great amount of unrelated earning power that Berkshire has.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Berkshire has more leeway in what it can do simply because it does have capital that's many times what its competitors have, and it also has earning power coming from a whole variety of unrelated areas â unrelated to insurance.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So it was not a negative judgment, in any way, on those two companies. It was not a negative judgment on their managements. But it was a â at least â a mildly negative judgment on the reinsurance business.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now, we have the ability at Berkshire to actually rearrange, to a degree â we are certainly affected by industry factors â but we have more flexibility in modifying business models, and we've operated that way, over the years, in insurance generally, and particularly in reinsurance.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, a Munich, a Swiss, all the major reinsurance companies, except for us, is pretty well tied to a given type of business model.

Sync Video to Paragraph

They don't really have as many options, in terms of where capital gets deployed. They have to continue down the present path.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I think they'll do fine. But I don't think they will do as fine in the next 10 years as they have in the last 10.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I don't think if we played the same game as we were playing the last 10, we would do as well, but we do have considerably more flexibility â in terms of how we conduct all of our insurance operations, but particularly in reinsurance â we have an extra string to our bow that the rest of the industry doesn't have.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The amount of capital that's come in to the reinsurance business â you know, it is no fun running a traditional reinsurance company and having money come in â particularly if you're in Europe â and have money come in, and look around you for investment choices and find out that a great many of the things that you were buying a few years ago now have negative yields.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The whole idea of float is it's supposed to be invested at a positive rate â a fairly substantial â positive rate.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And that game has been over for a while, and it looks like it will be, at least, unattractive, if not terrible, for a considerable period in the future.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah. But, you know, there's a lot of new capacity in reinsurance and there's a lot of very heavy competition.

Sync Video to Paragraph

A lot of people from finance have come over into reinsurance, and all the old competitors remained, too. Sync Video to Paragraph

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: The â to put it in terms of Economics 101 â basically, in reinsurance, supply has gone up and demand has not gone up.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And some of the supply is driven by investment managers who would like to establish something offshore where they don't have to pay taxes, and reinsurance is sort of the easiest beard â what you might call beard â behind which to actually engage in money management in a friendly tax jurisdiction.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And you can set up a reinsurance operation with very few people, by taking large chunks of what brokers may offer. It's not the greatest reinsurance in the world, and a couple of the operations that have done that have proven that statement to be right.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But nevertheless, it is a very, very easy way to have a disguised investment operation in a friendly tax jurisdiction. But that becomes supply in the reinsurance field, and supply has gone up relative to demand, and it looks to me like that will continue to be the case. And couple that with the poor returns on float, and it's not as good a business as it was.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The situation in Nevada is that, in terms of rooftop power, was that for the last few years, if you had a solar project on your roof, you could sell back excess power you generated to the grid at a price that was far, far, far above what we, as a utility, could buy it for elsewhere.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, you could sell it back, we'll say, at roughly 10 cents a kilowatt hour. And about 17,000 â maybe a few more now â about 17,000 people had rooftop installations.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Now they get â there were federal credits involved, but those usually got sold to other people, in terms of tax credits.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So they were being subsidized by the federal government, and that encouraged solar generation, as it's encouraged us to do solar generation and wind generation, as well.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But the people who had these 17,000 rooftop installations were selling back to the grid at 10 cents, roughly, a kilowatt hour, energy we could purchase or produce â either â but purchase elsewhere, too â for 3 1/2 cents, or thereabouts.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So, 99 percent of our consumers were being asked to subsidize the 1 percent that had solar units, by paying them a significantly â triple the market price, basically â of what we could otherwise buy electricity to sell to the 99 percent.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So then it's just a question of whether you wish to have the 99 percent subsidize the 1 percent.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And the public utility commission in Nevada, they had originally let this small amount of rooftop solar generation be allowed as an experiment with this 10 cent, roughly 10 cent, rebate.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And they decided that they did not believe that the 99 percent should be subsidizing the 1 percent.

Sync Video to Paragraph

There may â there's no question â that for solar to be competitive, just like wind, it needs subsidization. Costs are not yet at a level where it becomes competitive with natural gas, for example.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And who pays the subsidy gets to be a real question, if you want to encourage people to use renewables.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And, in general, the federal government has done it through tax subsidies, which means taxpayers, generally, throughout the country subsidize it.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And the public utility commission in Nevada decided that after seeing this experiment, they decided that it was not right for a million â well over a million â customers to be buying electricity at a price that subsidized the 17,000 people, and therefore increase the prices of electricity for the million.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And that question of who subsidizes renewables, and how much, is, you know, going to be a political question for a long time to come.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I personally think that if society is the one that's benefiting from the lack of â reduction of â greenhouse gases, that society should pick up the tab.
